The Cage Must Fall: Why Prisons Are a Moral and Practical Catastrophe Demanding Abolition

The prison system, as we know it, is not broken. It is functioning precisely as designed: a brutal, dehumanizing, and counterproductive machine of punishment that perpetuates harm, entrenches inequality, and fundamentally fails at its stated goals of justice, safety, and rehabilitation. It is not reform, but the complete abolition of prisons as punitive institutions, and their replacement with non-carceral systems centered on rehabilitation, restorative justice, and addressing root causes, that offers the only viable, ethical, and effective path toward a truly just and safe society. To cling to this obsolete paradigm is to choose endless cycles of violence over the possibility of genuine healing and prevention.

The foundational flaw of the prison-industrial complex is its core philosophy: retribution over restoration. Prisons are temples to vengeance, disguised as justice. This punitive logic is morally indefensible. Subjecting human beings to years of isolation, degradation, violence, and the systematic stripping of autonomy is not justice; it is state-sanctioned torture that inevitably degrades both the imprisoned and the society that sanctions it. Consider the harrowing reality: solitary confinement, proven to inflict severe psychological trauma akin to torture; rampant sexual assault; deliberate denial of healthcare leading to agonizing, preventable deaths; and the soul-crushing monotony designed to break the human spirit. How can a society claiming moral authority inflict such horrors? This is not safety; it is the normalization of cruelty within our most vulnerable communities. True justice demands accountability, yes, but accountability rooted in repairing harm and transforming relationships, not multiplying suffering. Restorative justice models, where offenders directly engage with victims and affected communities to understand harm, take responsibility, and collaboratively develop reparative plans, demonstrably yield higher victim satisfaction, lower recidivism, and foster community healing – outcomes prisons consistently fail to achieve.

Prisons are spectacularly ineffective at their purported aims, making them a colossal waste of human and financial capital. Recidivism rates hover around 70% globally, proving that prisons are not "correctional" but rather criminogenic institutions that equip individuals with deeper trauma, severed community ties, and insurmountable barriers to reintegration (housing, employment, voting rights). They fail to enhance public safety; by ripping individuals from families and communities, poisoning social networks, and failing to address the underlying drivers of crime, they actively generate future instability. Simultaneously, the financial burden is staggering: the United States alone spends over $80 billion annually on incarceration – money that could fund transformative community investments. Imagine redirecting even a fraction of this towards universal healthcare, quality education, affordable housing, and mental health services – the very root causes of crime that prisons ignore. Poverty, systemic racism, untreated mental illness, lack of opportunity, and community disinvestment are the fertile ground from which most crime grows. Prisons punish the symptoms while leaving the disease unchecked. Abolition demands we shift resources upstream: robust social safety nets, trauma-informed mental health crisis response teams (replacing police for non-violent crises), well-funded community centers, living-wage job programs, and transformative education initiatives. This is preventative justice in action.

Furthermore, the prison system is inextricably intertwined with systemic racism and class oppression. In the US and beyond, prisons disproportionately fill the cages of Black, Brown, and Indigenous people and the poor, reflecting biased policing, discriminatory sentencing (like the crack vs. powder cocaine disparity), and economic marginalization – not higher rates of criminal behavior. Mass incarceration is the logical descendant of slavery, Jim Crow, and convict leasing: a mechanism for social control and exploitation of racialized populations. Maintaining prisons perpetuates this violent legacy. Abolition is not race-neutral; it is a necessary step toward dismantling white supremacy embedded within our justice architecture. Non-carceral alternatives, developed with and by impacted communities, prioritize equity and address the specific historical and socioeconomic contexts that lead to harm.

Skeptics will inevitably cry, "What about violent offenders? What about public safety?" This is the fear-mongering that sustains the carceral state, but it ignores reality. Prisons are exceptionally poor at managing violence. They are hotbeds of violence within their walls, often exacerbating trauma and aggression. Crucially, most "violent" crimes are situational, context-driven, and deeply tied to the root causes mentioned above – poverty, lack of conflict resolution skills, cycles of trauma. Non-carceral responses are not about letting people "off the hook"; they are about more effective accountability. For acute situations, we can employ highly trained, unarmed community intervention specialists and crisis de-escalation teams. For serious harms, restorative processes can include community-based accountability plans with strict monitoring, mandatory reparations, therapeutic interventions, and community service – all far more likely to foster genuine change and reintegration than cage isolation. Countries like Norway, with its focus on humane, rehabilitative open units (functioning more as transitional communities than punitive cages) and robust social supports, boast recidivism rates below 20% and significantly lower rates of violent crime – proving safety and humanity are not mutually exclusive. Community-based responses, like the transformative justice initiatives pioneered in communities of color long before state systems acknowledged them, demonstrate that safety can be cultivated within communities through mutual aid, conflict resolution, and collective responsibility, not through external cages.

The call for abolition is not naive idealism; it is a pragmatic recognition of a failed 200-year experiment. Prisons are relics of a punitive past, ill-suited to address the complex social realities of the 21st century. They drain resources, destroy lives, fracture communities, and entrench injustice without delivering on the promise of safety. We possess the knowledge, the resources, and the moral imperative to build something radically better. By dismantling the prison industrial complex and investing relentlessly in non-carceral systems – systems centered on healing the trauma behind crime, repairing the harm caused by crime, and building thriving communities where crime is the rare exception, not the predictable outcome of neglect – we choose a future defined by justice, not vengeance; by community, not cages; by life, not control.

The cage is not justice. It is the symbol of our collective failure of imagination and compassion. It is time to tear it down, brick by crumbling brick, and build from the fertile ground of restoration, equity, and genuine human dignity. The path to true safety and justice lies not in deeper dungeons, but in the liberated spaces of community care and collective responsibility. Abolition is not just possible; it is the only ethical and effective path forward. Let us have the courage to walk it. The freedom of us all depends on it.

The push to abolish prisons and replace them with non-carceral, community-centered alternatives is rooted in decades of critique from abolitionist movements (e.g., Angela Davis, Ruth Wilson Gilmore), restorative justice pioneers (e.g., Howard Zehr), and evidence-based research. This isn’t about ignoring harm—it’s about redefining safety, justice, and accountability in ways prisons fail to achieve. Below is a balanced analysis of the core arguments, benefits, and practical reasoning behind this vision:

Why Prisons Fail (The Problem)

  1. Perpetuates Harm, Not Safety

    • Prisons are trauma incubators: 94% of incarcerated people experience violence (physical/sexual) in U.S. prisons. This trauma fuels recidivism (76% rearrested within 5 years).
    • Racial apartheid: Black Americans are incarcerated at 5x the rate of whites; Indigenous and Latinx communities face similar disparities. Prisons reinforce systemic racism.
    • Destroys communities: Mass incarceration drains economic/social resources from marginalized neighborhoods, creating cycles of poverty and distrust.

  2. Ineffective Rehabilitation

    • Isolation, dehumanization, and lack of meaningful programs leave people less prepared for reintegration. Only 9% of U.S. prisons offer college education—key to reducing recidivism.

  3. Ignores Root Causes
    Prisons treat symptoms (crime) while ignoring drivers: poverty, untreated mental illness (44% of incarcerated people have mental health issues), trauma, addiction, and lack of education/housing.

Core Principles of Non-Carceral Alternatives

Abolition isn’t "no accountability"—it’s reimagining accountability through:

  • Restorative Justice (RJ): Focuses on repairing harm, meeting victims’ needs, and addressing the causes of harm (e.g., victim-offender dialogues, community reparations).
  • Transformative Justice (TJ): Addresses systemic inequities (e.g., creating community-led safety networks, mental health crisis teams, housing access).
  • Preventive Investment: Redirecting prison funds to education, healthcare, housing, and job programs to prevent harm.

Documented Benefits of Abolitionist Models

✅ For Victims/Survivors

  • RJ programs show 85%+ victim satisfaction (vs. 40% in courts), with victims feeling heard and receiving tangible restitution.
  • Focus shifts from retribution to healing—e.g., a 2020 study in Criminology & Public Policy found RJ reduced PTSD symptoms in assault survivors by 60%.

✅ For Communities

  • Cost savings: Incarceration costs $81,000/year per person (NY) vs. $10,000 for community-based rehab. Savings fund housing, schools, and mental health services.
  • Stronger social fabric: Projects like Cure Violence (Chicago) treat violence as a health issue—using "violence interrupters" to mediate conflicts. Result: 67% homicide reduction in implemented areas.
  • Reduces racial disparities: Norway’s prison-free approach (max 21-year sentence) has 20% recidivism vs. U.S. 76%, with racial gaps nearly eliminated.

✅ For People Who Cause Harm

  • Lower recidivism: Canada’s Gladue courts (Indigenous-focused RJ) cut reoffending by 30% vs. regular courts.
  • Dignity and agency: Programs like S. Francisco’s INSPIRYS use trauma therapy and job training—recidivism drops to 15%.
  • Addresses root causes: Portugal’s drug decriminalization (replaced incarceration with health support) cut overdose deaths by 80%.

✅ Societal-Level Benefits

  • Breaks intergenerational trauma: Children of incarcerated parents are 5x more likely to go to prison. Abolition heals family units.
  • Aligns with global human rights: The U.S. (5% of world population) holds 20% of global prisoners—abolition brings alignment with UN standards.
  • Innovation in safety: Mental health crisis teams (e.g., CAHOOTS in Oregon) resolve 97% of calls without police, saving lives and costs.

Addressing Common Concerns

  • ❌ "What about violent offenders?"
    → Norway’s Halden Prison (often mislabeled "luxury") focuses on rehabilitation—even for murderers. Recidivism: 20% (vs. U.S. 76.6%). Community-based accountability for severe harm already exists: e.g., Mennonite RJ circles for sexual assault include mandated therapy, victim-led reparations, and community oversight—without cages.

  • ❌ "This is unrealistic utopianism"
    → Real-world pilots prove scalability:

    • New Zealand’s family group conferences (for youth crime) reduced reoffending by 30%.
    • Sweden’s open prisons (90% of prisons) have no bars; focus on work/education. Recidivism: 35% (vs. U.S. 76%).
    • Erie, CO banned local jails in 2021—using community safety teams instead. Violent crime dropped 22% in 2 years.

  • ❌ "It ignores victims’ need for justice"
    → RJ centers victims more than prisons ever do. In RJ, 90% of victims receive apologies/reparations; in prisons, victims rarely get restitution or closure (only 0.4% of court-ordered payments are collected in U.S. systems).

The Path Forward: Phased Abolition, Not Overnight Collapse

Abolitionists argue for dismantling prisons by building alternatives—not releasing people into unsafe voids:

  1. Decarcerate: End cash bail, legalize drugs, expunge records (e.g., CA reduced prison pop. by 33% since 2006).
  2. Invest: Redirect prison funds to mental health, housing, and violence interrupters (e.g., NYC’s $148M shift from jails to community services).
  3. Scale RJ: Mandate restorative practices in schools/courts (as seen in Scotland’s whole-system RJ adoption).
  4. Transform communities: Support grassroots TJ collectives (e.g., Creative Interventions toolkit for domestic violence cases).

Why This Vision Matters

Prisons were never designed for justice—they emerged from slavery (convict leasing) and colonial control. Abolition asks: "What do we need to be safe?" The answer lies in community care, not cages. As Ruth Wilson Gilmore states:
> "Abolition is not about the absence of prisons. It’s about the presence of everything we need to thrive."

Evidence confirms: when we address poverty, trauma, and inequality, harm decreases. Prisons are a $80B/year failure; non-carceral models offer a path to true safety—where accountability heals, communities flourish, and justice is transformative.

Beyond Bars: The Case for Abolishing Punitive Prisons

Introduction

The modern prison system stands as one of society's most profound failures—a monument to retribution that neither heals victims, rehabilitates offenders, nor creates safer communities. With over 10 million people incarcerated worldwide and recidivism rates exceeding 70% in many jurisdictions, the evidence is undeniable: prisons as punitive institutions have failed spectacularly at their stated objectives. It is time to acknowledge this failure and pursue a radical reimagining of justice—one that abolishes prisons and replaces them with systems centered on rehabilitation, restorative justice, and addressing the root causes of crime.

The Failure of Punitive Incarceration

Prisons Do Not Reduce Crime

The fundamental promise of incarceration—that locking people away makes communities safer—is demonstrably false. Countries with the highest incarceration rates do not have the lowest crime rates. The United States, which imprisons more people per capita than any nation in history, experiences crime rates comparable to or higher than countries with far more lenient systems. Norway, with its rehabilitation-focused approach and imprisonment rate of 50 per 100,000, has significantly lower crime rates than the U.S., with its rate of 700 per 100,000.

Research consistently shows that incarceration has, at best, a minimal deterrent effect. Most crimes occur impulsively or under circumstances where individuals are not weighing long-term consequences. The National Institute of Justice found that increasing sentence lengths has negligible impact on crime rates. What deters crime is the certainty of being caught—not the severity of punishment—combined with addressing underlying factors like poverty, lack of opportunity, and untreated mental illness.

Prisons Create More Crime Than They Prevent

Far from reducing criminality, prisons function as crime incubators. They concentrate individuals in violent, dehumanizing environments where survival often requires adopting criminal behaviors and affiliations. People emerge from prison with trauma, weakened family bonds, criminal networks, and the stigma of a conviction that bars them from employment, housing, and civic participation.

The recidivism statistics tell the story: within five years of release, approximately 76% of formerly incarcerated individuals are rearrested. This revolving door demonstrates that prisons don't address the factors that lead to criminal behavior—they exacerbate them. Each cycle of incarceration deepens poverty, severs community ties, and increases the likelihood of future offenses.

The Moral Bankruptcy of Punitive Justice

The punitive model rests on the premise that inflicting suffering on those who have caused harm creates justice. This logic is morally incoherent. Adding more suffering to the world does nothing to heal the original harm. Victims of crime consistently report that what they need most is acknowledgment of their pain, answers to their questions, and assurance that similar harm won't occur again. The criminal justice system provides none of this—victims are sidelined while the state pursues punishment in their name.

Moreover, the cruelty inherent in modern incarceration—the isolation, violence, sexual assault, inadequate healthcare, and psychological torture—constitutes harm far beyond any legitimate social purpose. We have constructed a system that brutalizes human beings, often for non-violent offenses, and calls it justice.

The Social Construction of Crime and Punishment

Crime as a Symptom of Social Failure

The majority of behaviors we criminalize stem directly from poverty, inequality, lack of opportunity, untreated mental illness, and substance abuse disorders. Approximately 65% of incarcerated individuals meet criteria for substance use disorders, yet only 11% receive treatment during incarceration. An estimated 37% have been diagnosed with mental health conditions, rates far exceeding the general population.

Property crimes, which constitute a substantial portion of the prison population, are overwhelmingly committed by people experiencing economic desperation. We have criminalized poverty itself—making it illegal to be homeless, to panhandle, to survive through informal economies when formal opportunities are unavailable. Our response to social inequality has been incarceration rather than addressing the inequality itself.

The Selectivity of Criminalization

Our society makes choices about which harmful behaviors to criminalize and which to excuse or ignore. Corporate executives who knowingly market addictive opioids, creating an epidemic that kills tens of thousands annually, face minimal consequences. Wage theft—employers stealing earned wages from workers—amounts to more monetary loss than all robberies, burglaries, and auto thefts combined, yet is treated as a civil rather than criminal matter.

Environmental destruction, financial fraud by the wealthy, and state violence rarely result in incarceration, while poverty-related offenses fill our prisons. This selective enforcement reveals that our criminal justice system is not fundamentally about preventing harm—it is a mechanism for managing poverty and maintaining social hierarchies.

The Case for Abolition and Transformation

Learning from Alternative Models

We need not speculate about alternatives—they exist and succeed. Norway's system, which treats prisoners with dignity and focuses entirely on rehabilitation, achieves a recidivism rate of just 20%, the lowest in the world. Their maximum security facilities resemble college campuses more than American prisons, offering education, vocational training, therapy, and gradual reintegration into society.

Indigenous communities worldwide have practiced restorative justice for millennia, bringing together those who caused harm, those harmed, and the broader community to address root causes, repair damage, and reintegrate all parties. New Zealand's incorporation of Maori restorative practices into their youth justice system reduced youth incarceration by 80% while improving outcomes for both victims and offenders.

Countries that decriminalized drug possession—most notably Portugal—have seen dramatic reductions in drug-related deaths, HIV transmission, and drug use itself by treating addiction as a health issue rather than a criminal matter. These models demonstrate that non-punitive approaches achieve what prisons cannot: genuine reduction in harmful behavior.

A Framework for Transformation

Abolishing prisons requires building robust alternatives addressing different circumstances:

For addressing harmful behavior:

  • Restorative justice processes that bring together affected parties to determine accountability measures, restitution, and prevention
  • Community-based accountability programs where individuals remain in their communities under supervision while making amends
  • Intensive therapeutic interventions for those whose behavior stems from trauma or mental health conditions
  • Immediate crisis response teams trained in de-escalation and mental health support, replacing police in many situations

For addressing root causes:

  • Universal access to mental health and substance abuse treatment
  • Guaranteed housing, recognizing that stable housing prevents crime more effectively than incarceration
  • Living-wage employment and universal basic income to eliminate poverty-driven crime
  • Free education and vocational training as alternatives to illicit economies
  • Investment in communities—particularly those historically over-policed and under-resourced

For accountability without cages:

  • Electronic monitoring for those who pose flight risks, when necessary
  • Intensive supervision programs in community settings
  • Mandatory education, therapy, or community service rather than incarceration
  • Asset-based restitution to victims of financial crimes
  • Restorative processes focused on harm repair rather than punishment

Addressing Difficult Cases

The most common objection to prison abolition concerns individuals who pose genuine danger to others. This objection deserves serious consideration, but it doesn't justify the current system.

First, truly dangerous individuals constitute a small fraction of the prison population. The vast majority are incarcerated for non-violent offenses, and even among those convicted of violent crimes, most pose no continuing threat. Risk assessment tools, while imperfect, can identify the small number who require separation from the community.

For this small population, we can create secure facilities that look nothing like current prisons—therapeutic environments focused entirely on addressing the factors that led to violence and preparing for eventual community reintegration. These would be trauma-informed mental health facilities with extensive programming, not punishment chambers. The goal remains rehabilitation and healing, not suffering.

Moreover, we must acknowledge that prisons currently fail to contain dangerous people effectively. Violence is rampant within prisons, and individuals eventually return to communities, often more dangerous than when they entered. If public safety is the genuine concern, the current system cannot be defended.

Economic and Social Benefits of Abolition

The Financial Case

The United States alone spends over $182 billion annually on incarceration when including all associated costs. This represents an astronomical opportunity cost—money that could provide free college education for all, universal healthcare, or eliminate homelessness several times over. The average cost of incarcerating one person for one year ranges from $30,000 to $60,000—far exceeding the cost of providing housing, education, healthcare, and social services.

Comprehensive rehabilitation and restorative programs are significantly less expensive than incarceration while producing dramatically better outcomes. Norway spends roughly $100,000 per prisoner annually—more than the U.S. per capita—but saves money in the long term through low recidivism rates and productive citizens.

When individuals remain in communities, contributing economically and maintaining family bonds, society benefits across generations. The children of incarcerated parents are six times more likely to be incarcerated themselves—breaking this cycle creates compounding social benefits.

Healing Communities

Mass incarceration has devastated communities, particularly Black, Latino, and Indigenous communities subjected to discriminatory enforcement. Entire neighborhoods have been destabilized by removing fathers, mothers, siblings, and children—creating trauma, breaking economic networks, and depleting communities of human potential.

Abolition means reinvesting resources into these communities: building schools instead of prisons, funding youth programs instead of prosecution, providing treatment instead of punishment. When communities receive the resources currently devoted to caging their members, transformation becomes possible.

Addressing Counterarguments

"Some people deserve punishment"

This retributivist logic assumes that state-inflicted suffering creates justice, but this premise fails both logically and empirically. Punishment doesn't undo harm—it adds more harm. Even if we accept that some deserve to suffer (a morally questionable premise), organizing society around inflicting suffering corrupts everyone involved. Guards, administrators, and society itself are brutalized by maintaining systems of deliberate cruelty.

Moreover, the concept of "deserving" punishment assumes equal culpability while ignoring vastly different circumstances. Someone who steals because they're hungry faces the same legal system as someone who steals for entertainment, despite profoundly different moral situations. A system focused on addressing needs and repairing harm serves justice better than one obsessed with deserved suffering.

"Victims deserve to see offenders punished"

Research on victims' needs consistently shows that most prioritize safety, acknowledgment, answers, and prevention over punishment. Victims are frequently dissatisfied with the criminal justice system because it sidelines them while professionals pursue punishment. Restorative justice processes, which center victims' actual needs and voices, produce significantly higher victim satisfaction rates than traditional prosecution.

Some victims do want punishment, but organizing society's response to harm around vengeance creates policy that serves neither victims' long-term interests nor public safety. Systems centered on healing and prevention better honor victims by working to ensure no one else suffers similar harm.

"This is too radical and will never happen"

Every transformative social change—abolishing slavery, recognizing women's rights, ending Jim Crow segregation—was dismissed as impossibly radical until it happened. The current system is unsustainable: financially draining, morally bankrupt, and demonstrably failing at its stated purposes. When systems fail comprehensively, radical reimagining becomes necessary.

Moreover, abolition is not an overnight process but a horizon toward which we work. Each step—decriminalizing drugs, investing in mental health treatment, closing prisons as populations decrease, implementing restorative justice—moves us toward abolition while immediately improving lives. The goal orients the direction; the journey consists of concrete, incremental changes.

Conclusion: Choosing Justice Over Vengeance

The choice before us is clear: continue pouring resources into a failed system that creates suffering without producing safety, or build something fundamentally different—a system that addresses harm by healing rather than adding more harm.

Prison abolition is not about ignoring harm or abandoning accountability. It is about taking both more seriously than the current system does. It means asking what actually prevents crime—and having the courage to implement those solutions. It means measuring justice by healing rather than suffering inflicted.

The evidence is overwhelming: rehabilitation works, restorative justice works, addressing root causes works. Punishment fails. We have the knowledge, resources, and models to create genuine justice. What we need is the moral courage to abandon a system that has never worked and build one worthy of a society that values human dignity.

The walls must come down—not because those inside are innocent, but because the cages themselves are the crime. Justice requires nothing less than abolition.

Prompt:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of the complete abolition of prisons as punitive institutions, advocating for their dismantling and replacement with non-carceral systems centered on rehabilitation, restorative justice, and addressing the root causes of crime.
Model Response:

Prisons, as punitive institutions, should be completely abolished and replaced with non-carceral systems centered on rehabilitation, restorative justice, and addressing the root causes of harm. Their continued existence rests on myths: that cages make us safer, that punishment heals wounds, and that human beings are disposable when they break the law. A careful look at history, evidence, and existing alternatives shows those myths are wrong—and that maintaining mass incarceration is a moral, social, and practical failure.

I. The Origins and Logic of Prisons Are Fundamentally Flawed

Modern prisons are not timeless or natural; they are relatively recent inventions. They emerged in the 18th and 19th centuries alongside industrial capitalism, colonial expansion, and racialized social control.

  • Discipline for the industrial age: As societies shifted from agrarian economies to wage labor, states needed new ways to control surplus and “unruly” populations—formerly enslaved people, the poor, the unemployed, migrants. Prison became a tool to regulate labor, not simply to address harm.
  • Racial and colonial control: In the United States and many other countries, imprisonment grew as a replacement for slavery, convict leasing, and other explicitly racist systems. Laws were written and enforced in ways that criminalized Black people, Indigenous people, and colonized populations, turning prisons into engines of racial domination.
  • Pathologizing poverty: Vagrancy laws, debtors’ prisons, and similar mechanisms criminalized poverty, homelessness, mental illness, and addiction—problems rooted in economic and social structures rather than “individual evil.”

From their very inception, prisons were less about safety and more about managing, warehousing, and disciplining groups deemed “undesirable.” The idea that they exist primarily to prevent harm or deliver justice is historically inaccurate.

II. Prisons Fail on Their Own Stated Goals

Even if we accepted the premise that prisons should exist to protect people and reduce crime, they fail by their own measures.

1. They do not effectively reduce crime or recidivism

Across countries with heavy reliance on incarceration, recidivism is high. Many people reoffend not because prison “wasn’t harsh enough,” but because:

  • They leave with no housing, few employment prospects, and untreated trauma.
  • They are stigmatized by a criminal record that blocks them from jobs, education, and social support.
  • The environment of prison trains people to survive through violence, hypervigilance, manipulation, and distrust—behaviors harmful in ordinary social life.

By contrast, countries and jurisdictions that reduce incarceration and prioritize rehabilitation (e.g., many Nordic countries, some Latin American and European local programs) have lower recidivism rates and lower levels of violent crime over time. Evidence repeatedly shows:

  • Punishment severity is a weak deterrent.
  • Certainty and swiftness of non-carceral, proportionate responses coupled with robust social supports are far more effective at reducing future harm.

2. They do not deliver justice for victims and communities

The prison system frames justice as a transaction between the state and the person who caused harm, with the victim often sidelined. For many victims and survivors:

  • The formal system is retraumatizing: adversarial, impersonal, and focused on “winning a case” rather than healing.
  • They have little say in what accountability should look like or what they need to feel safe and supported (therapy, financial repair, community acknowledgment, guarantees the harm won’t recur).
  • Long sentences commonly do nothing to address their material needs—medical bills, lost wages, relocation costs, childcare, trauma treatment.

Many survivors report feeling dissatisfied or even worse after going through the criminal legal process. Prisons offer symbolic retribution, not actual repair.

3. They do not keep society safer in the long term

Politicians often point to incarceration as the reason crime drops. But large-scale research indicates that:

  • Most crime trends correlate more strongly with social factors—economic conditions, social welfare systems, demographics, and inequality—than with incarceration rates.
  • There are diminishing returns: beyond a certain point, locking more people up yields almost no added safety benefit, but generates enormous social and economic costs.
  • Incarceration destabilizes communities, especially marginalized ones: removing parents and wage-earners, spreading trauma, and normalizing state violence—all factors that contribute to cycles of harm.

When whole neighborhoods are heavily policed and incarcerated, the state subjects them to chronic trauma and surveillance instead of investing in housing, health care, jobs, and education—the very things shown to prevent harm.

III. Prisons Are Inherently Violent and Dehumanizing

Even if prisons could be made more humane, their basic structure rests on caging human beings and stripping them of autonomy. This generates systemic, inescapable harms.

1. Institutionalized violence

Prisons rely on:

  • Force and coercion to maintain control: physical violence, threat of solitary confinement, loss of contact with family.
  • Sexual abuse and exploitation, both by other incarcerated people and by staff, which flourish in environments of total power imbalance.
  • Psychological degradation: humiliation, constant surveillance, arbitrary discipline, and an atmosphere of fear.

These are not aberrations but predictable outcomes of creating environments where one group has nearly absolute power over another.

2. Psychological damage and trauma

Extended confinement and social isolation are well-documented to cause or worsen:

  • Depression, anxiety, and PTSD
  • Cognitive decline and difficulty with emotional regulation
  • Increased risk of suicide and self-harm

Solitary confinement—a common disciplinary measure—is widely recognized by psychologists, human rights organizations, and even some courts as a form of torture when used beyond very short periods. Yet it remains routine.

People often leave prison more traumatized, less capable of healthy relationships, and less able to navigate everyday life—precisely the opposite of what a society seeking safety should want.

3. Dehumanization as a principle

To justify caging people, the system must frame them as fundamentally different and less deserving: “criminals,” “offenders,” “predators.” This dehumanization:

  • Makes it easier to ignore abuse and neglect behind walls.
  • Reinforces racism, classism, ableism, and xenophobia, since those disproportionately targeted by the system are already stigmatized.
  • Leaks into public life—encouraging a punitive political culture that favors punishment over care in many domains (schools, welfare, immigration, mental health).

A system built on dehumanization cannot be fully reformed; its core logic is incompatible with dignity and equality.

IV. Prisons Entrench Inequality and Structural Injustice

Prisons amplify existing inequalities instead of addressing their root causes.

1. Criminalization of poverty and marginalization

The criminal legal system systematically targets those with the least resources:

  • Poor individuals are more likely to be arrested, convicted, and given harsh sentences; they also cannot afford quality legal representation or bail.
  • Racial and ethnic minorities, particularly Black, Indigenous, and other marginalized communities, face discriminatory policing, charging, and sentencing.
  • People with mental illness or disability are funneled into jails and prisons due to inadequate community mental health resources.
  • Survivors of violence, especially women, LGBTQ+ people, and marginalized groups, are frequently criminalized for survival strategies or for defending themselves.

Thus, prisons act as repositories for social problems that society refuses to address: poverty, trauma, addiction, racism, homelessness, and exclusion.

2. Perpetuating intergenerational harm

Incarceration doesn’t just affect individuals; it reverberates through families and communities:

  • Children of incarcerated parents face higher risks of poverty, foster care placement, homelessness, and involvement with the criminal legal system.
  • Communities with high incarceration rates experience weakened social networks, depressed local economies, and the normalization of state violence.
  • Returning citizens often encounter legal barriers (to housing, voting, employment, education, benefits) that keep them in a permanent underclass.

Prison-based “public safety” is a myth that trades the safety of wealthy and powerful groups for the continued insecurity of poor and marginalized ones.

V. The Myth of “Necessary” Prisons: Addressing Common Objections

Abolition does not mean “doing nothing about harm.” It means rejecting cages and punishment as the default response, and building systems that actually prevent and repair harm. Several common objections deserve serious answers.

Objection 1: “What about violent crime and dangerous people?”

This is the most frequently raised concern—and it is valid to care deeply about violence. But prisons are not the only, nor the best, way to address it.

  • Most violence is not random; it arises from patterns of abuse, inequality, and social dislocation.
  • Many people convicted of violent offenses age out of violence and do not pose an ongoing threat if they receive treatment, support, and a path back into community life.
  • Programs that focus on violence interruption, trauma treatment, mental health care, and conflict mediation reduce violent crime more effectively than increased incarceration.

For the small subset of people who presently pose a serious, continuing risk, abolition does not forbid separation. It insists that:

  • Any separation be non-punitive, therapeutic, and time-limited where possible.
  • Conditions be oriented toward care, accountability, and transformation—not degradation or warehousing.
  • The ultimate goal remains reintegration, not permanent exile.

In other words, the question is not whether we can ever temporarily restrict someone’s liberty, but whether that restriction must take the form of violent, punitive, dehumanizing institutions. Abolitionists argue it must not.

Objection 2: “Without prisons, won’t people think they can do anything?”

Deterrence is often overstated. People commit harm, especially serious violence, under conditions where:

  • They are acting impulsively, under emotional or substance-related influence.
  • They believe they won’t be caught.
  • They are in contexts of chronic violence where harm feels normal or inevitable.

The threat of distant imprisonment cannot meaningfully deter many of these situations. What does deter harm is:

  • Strong, supportive communities with norms against violence.
  • Stable housing, income, and education.
  • Accessible mental health and addiction services.
  • Swift, certain, but proportionate and restorative responses to early or lower-level harm.

Replacing prisons doesn’t eliminate consequences; it changes them—from abstract, delayed, punitive suffering to concrete, immediate, reparative accountability.

Objection 3: “Can’t we just reform prisons—make them more humane?”

Decades of “reform” have not changed the core reality: prisons remain sites of violence, racial control, trauma, and deprivation. Reforms often:

  • Expand the system’s legitimacy and budget (“better prisons” justify more imprisonment).
  • Create minor improvements for some while leaving the fundamental structure—caging human beings—as is.
  • Introduce new forms of control like electronic monitoring and community supervision that expand surveillance without shrinking incarceration.

If the underlying problem is the logic of punishment and confinement, then building “nicer” cages doesn’t solve it. Abolition demands that we shift from punishing people to transforming the conditions that produce harm.

VI. What Could Replace Prisons? A Non-Carceral Framework

Abolishing prisons requires building robust alternative systems. This is not a utopian wish; many components already exist in different places at different scales. The task is to generalize, strengthen, and connect them.

1. Addressing root causes: social and economic justice

Most crime—especially property crime and many forms of interpersonal harm—is tightly linked to unmet needs and structural violence. A non-carceral approach centers:

  • Universal basic needs: stable housing, food, health care (including mental health and addiction services), and education.
  • Decent work and income: living wages, strong labor protections, and accessible job training.
  • Community infrastructure: safe public spaces, youth centers, libraries, cultural institutions, and recreation.

When people have their basic needs met, supportive relationships, and meaningful opportunities, the incentive and pressure to engage in harmful behavior drops dramatically.

2. Restorative and transformative justice

Restorative and transformative justice practices focus on repairing harm and changing conditions, not on inflicting suffering.

Key principles:

  • Centering those harmed: asking what they need to feel safe, respected, and supported—emotional support, financial restitution, community acknowledgment, safety planning, etc.
  • Meaningful accountability: The person who caused harm must take responsibility, understand the impact, and participate in making things right as far as possible.
  • Community involvement: Families, neighbors, coworkers, and community members participate in creating safety plans, support networks, and changes in local conditions.

Concrete models include:

  • Restorative circles and conferences, where all parties meet with trained facilitators to discuss harm and create a resolution plan.
  • Community-based accountability groups that support individuals in changing behavior (e.g., domestic violence intervention programs, transformative justice pods).
  • Victim-offender mediation programs that operate outside or alongside the formal legal system.

Studies of many such programs show high satisfaction among survivors, reduced recidivism, and more durable healing than traditional punishment.

3. Health-based responses to addiction, mental illness, and trauma

A large share of criminalized behavior is linked to untreated or poorly treated health conditions:

  • Substance use disorders
  • Mental health crises and chronic conditions
  • Unaddressed trauma, including childhood abuse and exposure to violence

Instead of jails and prisons, we need:

  • Crisis response teams staffed by mental health professionals and peer workers, not or not only armed police.
  • Voluntary, accessible treatment for addiction and mental illness, with harm-reduction approaches (e.g., supervised consumption sites, medication-assisted therapy).
  • Trauma-informed care and long-term therapy accessible regardless of income.
  • Safe housing options for people in crisis, rather than criminalization of homelessness or public disorder.

Countries that treat these as public health issues rather than crimes consistently achieve better health and safety outcomes.

4. Limited, non-punitive secure care for exceptional cases

Abolition does not require ignoring genuine, ongoing threats of serious harm. For a small minority of cases where robust supports, treatment, and community processes do not prevent ongoing lethal or severe violence, society may still need:

  • Secure, therapeutic environments where people can be temporarily or, in rare cases, longer-term separated.
  • Strong, enforceable safeguards for rights, dignity, and due process.
  • Regular review and a presumption in favor of release when risk can be safely managed.
  • Conditions focused on rehabilitation, education, therapy, and relationship-building, not punishment or deprivation.

The crucial distinction is this: these are not prisons in the sense of punitive warehousing; they are highly regulated care facilities oriented toward safety and eventual reintegration, with strict restrictions on their use and scope.

VII. Abolition as a Practical, Gradual Project

Abolishing prisons is not an overnight switch; it is a political, social, and cultural project that unfolds in stages.

1. Shrinking the system’s reach

  • Decriminalize poverty-related offenses, low-level drug use, sex work, and other consensual activities.
  • End cash bail and pretrial detention for most offenses.
  • Drastically reduce sentence lengths and eliminate mandatory minimums.
  • Expand diversion programs that route people away from the criminal legal system into community-based supports.

2. Divesting from punishment and investing in care

  • Reallocate funding from police, jails, and prisons to housing, education, health care, and community services.
  • Fund restorative and transformative justice programs and community accountability projects.
  • Support survivors with robust resources separate from the punitive system.

3. Transforming norms and culture

  • Change how schools, families, workplaces, and media talk about conflict, harm, and accountability—shifting from blame and exile to repair and responsibility.
  • Teach conflict resolution, emotional literacy, and nonviolent communication as core skills.
  • Challenge the narratives that equate punishment with justice and equate safety with policing and incarceration.

Abolition is about building the conditions under which prisons become not only obsolete but widely recognized as unnecessary and unacceptable.

VIII. The Moral Imperative: We Can Do Better Than Cages

At its core, the argument for abolishing prisons is moral as well as practical.

  • Every person is more than the worst thing they have done. A system that fixes people’s identities around their harm denies human capacity for change and growth.
  • Punishment does not heal. Inflicting suffering on those who cause harm does not undo that harm or prevent future violence; it often compounds trauma and alienation.
  • Human dignity is non-negotiable. Stripping human beings of autonomy, intimacy, movement, and meaningful connection as a default response to harm is an affront to any serious commitment to human rights.

We already know that other approaches work better to reduce harm, support survivors, and build safer communities. Many of the necessary tools—restorative justice practices, public health frameworks, social safety nets, violence interruption, and community-based supports—are in active use and success around the world. The barrier is not feasibility; it is imagination, political will, and the willingness to let go of punishment as our reflex.

Prisons are not a natural or inevitable feature of human society. They are a specific, historically contingent response to social problems—one that has proven massively destructive, discriminatory, and ineffective. To cling to them in the face of better alternatives is to choose cruelty and failure over care and possibility.

Abolishing prisons as punitive institutions is not about abandoning safety; it is about finally taking it seriously. It is a commitment to build a world where harms are less likely to occur—and when they do, where our response is guided by healing, accountability, and the unshakeable conviction that no one is disposable.

Prompt:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons to adopt the policy of entirely abolishing prisons and replacing them with non-carceral models focused on rehabilitation, restorative justice, and community-based accountability.
Model Response:

Abolishing prisons and replacing them with non-carceral, rehabilitation- and community-based systems is usually argued for on three levels:

  1. Moral/ethical – prisons are seen as inherently harmful and incompatible with a just society.
  2. Practical/effectiveness – prisons often fail at their stated goals (reducing harm, crime, and fear), while alternatives can work better.
  3. Structural/political – prisons are understood as part of broader systems of inequality, racism, and social control.

Below is a structured overview of the main supposed benefits and reasons people give for a fully non-carceral model.

1. Harm Reduction and Human Dignity

A. Prisons as inherently harmful

Critics argue that prisons:

  • Produce trauma: isolation, violence, abuse, and lack of autonomy create or worsen trauma, mental illness, and addiction.
  • Destroy social bonds: incarceration removes people from families, children, and communities, which are actually key protective factors against future harm.
  • Teach survival, not accountability: prison culture often rewards toughness, denial, and distrust, not reflection, empathy, or responsibility.

From this perspective, even “humane” prisons remain systems of coercive confinement that:

  • Treat people as risks to be managed rather than human beings capable of change.
  • Violate basic ethical commitments to dignity, bodily integrity, and freedom of movement.

B. Non-carceral models as more consistent with human rights

Alternatives like restorative justice, transformative justice, and community accountability aim to:

  • Recognize the personhood and potential of everyone involved, including those who caused harm.
  • Address the needs of victims/survivors (safety, validation, material support) rather than centering punishment.
  • Ground responses in consent, negotiation, and repair, not forced confinement.

The ethical claim: a society committed to human rights should prefer systems that minimize coercion and maximize autonomy, support, and dialogue.

2. Effectiveness: Safety, Recidivism, and Public Well‑Being

A. Prisons often fail at reducing future harm

Research from many countries shows:

  • High recidivism: a large share of people leaving prison are rearrested or returned to prison within a few years.
  • Criminogenic effects: incarceration can make people more likely to offend (through trauma, stigma, loss of lawful livelihood, and immersion in criminalized networks).
  • Limited deterrence: harsher sentences don’t reliably reduce crime compared to more certain but less severe responses; many offenses are impulsive, desperate, or driven by addiction or mental illness.

So, from an effectiveness standpoint, prisons are frequently seen as:

  • Bad at changing behavior.
  • Bad at preventing future harm.
  • Expensive relative to the safety benefits they actually deliver.

B. Rehabilitation and treatment work better when not carceral

Non-carceral approaches emphasize:

  • Housing, healthcare, mental health care, and addiction treatment as central crime-prevention strategies.
  • Education and employment support to address structural drivers of lawbreaking.
  • Therapeutic interventions (e.g., trauma-informed counseling, cognitive-behavioral programs) delivered in community settings.

Evidence from specific programs and countries suggests:

  • Well-designed treatment, diversion, and support programs can significantly reduce reoffending.
  • Community-based mental health and substance use treatment often performs better than prison-based programs, because it keeps people in their support networks and avoids additional trauma.
  • Stable housing and income are among the most powerful predictors of desistance from crime.

The underlying claim: if the goal is fewer harms in the future, money and effort are better spent on support, treatment, and opportunity than on cages.

3. Centering Survivors and Harmed Communities

A. Punishment vs. meeting survivors’ actual needs

Many people who’ve survived violence or theft report that what they want includes:

  • Safety (protection from further harm).
  • Acknowledgment of the harm, not denial.
  • Answers and understanding (why did this happen?).
  • Material repair (e.g., medical costs, lost wages, replacement of stolen or destroyed property).
  • Validation and community support.

Traditional criminal legal systems and prisons:

  • Often exclude survivors from decisions and processes.
  • Give them little control over outcomes.
  • May retraumatize them through adversarial procedures and cross-examination.

B. Restorative and transformative justice as survivor-centered

Non-carceral models aim to:

  • Involve survivors directly in shaping what accountability and repair look like (if they want to participate).
  • Offer dialogue, apology, and narrative: opportunities to be heard, ask questions, and receive acknowledgment.
  • Provide ongoing support: therapy, housing, medical care, community accompaniment.
  • Focus on restitution and concrete repair (where possible), rather than abstract state-imposed punishment.

The claimed benefit: these approaches can more genuinely address harm and support healing, rather than symbolically punishing in the name of the state.

4. Addressing Root Causes Instead of Symptoms

A. Crime as a symptom of social conditions

Abolitionist arguments emphasize that much lawbreaking is driven by:

  • Poverty and economic inequality.
  • Racism, colonialism, and marginalization.
  • Unstable housing, poor education, and joblessness.
  • Unaddressed trauma, mental illness, and addiction.
  • Gendered violence and patriarchy.

Prisons, in this view, treat the visible symptom (individual acts of harm) rather than the structural conditions that gave rise to them.

B. Non-carceral models target conditions, not just acts

Instead of pouring money into incarceration, the alternative is to invest in:

  • Universal or robust social welfare (income supports, child care, unemployment protections).
  • Quality education and job pathways in marginalized communities.
  • Accessible mental health and addiction services.
  • Violence interruption and community-based safety programs.
  • Housing-first policies.

Evidence across countries shows that:

  • Societies with lower inequality, better welfare states, and robust services often have lower crime rates and less need for harsh punishment.
  • Early intervention and social support are usually more cost-effective than reacting later with policing and imprisonment.

The premise: if you remove the conditions that foster harm, you need less coercive control—so a non-carceral model is both cause-focused and preventative.

5. Racial and Social Justice

A. Prisons as tools of racial and class control

Historically and in the present, prison systems often:

  • Disproportionately target racialized, colonized, and poor communities via policing, prosecution, and sentencing.
  • Reflect historical continuities with slavery, colonialism, and segregation (e.g., Black and Indigenous overrepresentation).
  • Reproduce intergenerational disadvantage: incarceration of parents leads to worse outcomes for children, communities, and neighborhoods.

Even with reforms, critics argue that:

  • Bias is embedded in every stage: from who is stopped and searched to bail decisions to plea deals to sentencing.
  • Prisons function as a warehouse for those made surplus by economic and social systems.

B. Abolition as part of dismantling structural oppression

Replacing prisons with non-carceral models is framed as:

  • A step toward dismantling institutional racism and class control.
  • A move toward decriminalizing poverty, addiction, and survival behaviors.
  • A chance to redesign safety systems so marginalized communities are not primarily policed and punished, but resourced and supported.

The benefit is not only reducing formal incarceration, but also transforming how state power is used: away from criminalization, toward redistribution and care.

6. Economic Arguments

A. Prisons are extremely expensive

Imprisonment requires:

  • Building, maintaining, and securing facilities.
  • Paying correctional staff, health care, food, and transportation.
  • Long-term costs: people leaving prison have worse employment and health outcomes, which create downstream public costs.

On a per-person basis, incarcerating someone is often:

  • Far more expensive than funding high-quality community treatment, education, or housing.
  • A misallocation of resources if it doesn’t substantially reduce future harm.

B. Non-carceral models can be cheaper and higher-yield

Advocates argue that:

  • Redirecting prison budgets to prevention, treatment, housing, and restorative processes can provide more safety per dollar.
  • Investing in social services and infrastructure yields broader benefits (health, education, productivity) beyond crime reduction.

Even where alternatives require substantial funding, they:

  • Build lasting capacity in communities.
  • Avoid the economic drain of mass incarceration (lost labor, weakened families, community destabilization).

7. Community Empowerment and Democratic Control

A. Current systems are top-down and distant

Prison-based justice is typically:

  • State-centric: decisions are made by prosecutors, judges, corrections officials, not communities or survivors.
  • Geographically removed: prisons are often far from the communities most affected, making meaningful participation hard.
  • Technocratic: people most impacted have limited say in designing safety systems.

B. Non-carceral models center community agency

Community-based accountability and transformative justice emphasize:

  • Local decision-making: community members co-design processes for intervention, accountability, and support.
  • Building conflict resolution and mediation skills within neighborhoods, workplaces, schools, and families.
  • Creating new institutions—peace circles, neighborhood councils, crisis response teams—rooted in local knowledge and trust.

The claimed benefit: safety becomes a collective practice, not something outsourced to distant institutions; people gain experience and capacity to handle conflict without violence or state coercion.

8. Flexibility and Creativity vs. One-Size-Fits-All Punishment

A. Prison is a blunt instrument

Prison essentially offers one tool: removal from society for a set period. This is:

  • Poorly matched to the huge variety of harms (from nonviolent property offenses to complex interpersonal violence).
  • Unable to address interpersonal dynamics, histories of trauma, or specific community contexts.
  • Very limited in what it can require by way of positive action (e.g., genuine restitution, community repair), beyond time served.

B. Non-carceral approaches allow tailored responses

Without the prison default, systems can:

  • Design responses specific to particular kinds of harm (e.g., intimate partner violence, youth conflict, neighborhood disputes).
  • Combine multiple tools: restitution, treatment, community monitoring, skill-building, and long-term support.
  • Focus on behaviors and relationships, not just “offenses,” aiming for changed patterns rather than box-checking punishment.

This flexibility is argued to be:

  • Better for safety (because interventions are targeted and adaptive).
  • Better for fairness (because context and needs matter).

9. Expansion of Imagination and Political Possibility

A. Abolition as a horizon, not just a policy tweak

Prison abolitionists often argue:

  • As long as prisons exist as a “normal” option, policymakers will default to them instead of doing the harder work of building alternatives.
  • Imagining a world without prisons forces society to rethink what safety, accountability, and justice mean at a deep level.
  • Abolition is as much about creating new institutions and cultures as it is about tearing old ones down.

B. Building non-carceral infrastructure now

The benefits of committing to an abolitionist horizon include:

  • Directing energy and resources toward new practices rather than endless reforms of a system seen as fundamentally flawed.
  • Encouraging experimentation with peer-led, survivor-led, and community-driven models of response to harm.
  • Making it more likely that, over time, prisons become obsolete because social, economic, and cultural changes reduce the perceived need for them.

10. Addressing Concerns About Serious Violence

A common challenge is: what about people who commit severe, repeated, or predatory violence?

Abolitionist or non-carceral arguments respond by asserting that:

  • Even now, prisons often fail to prevent or transform such violence; they may delay it, but don’t address its roots.
  • People who commit serious harm are frequently themselves shaped by long histories of abuse, deprivation, and trauma, which prison rarely addresses.
  • Society could invest in intensive, high-support, secure but non-prison environments that are:
    • Therapeutic rather than punitive.
    • Focused on behavior change, not pure incapacitation.
    • Bound by strict rights, independent oversight, and strong exit pathways.

Some abolitionists accept that some form of secure separation may remain necessary for a very small group of people for some time, but argue:

  • This should not take the form of current prisons.
  • The overall system should be built around care, prevention, and repair, not mass incarceration.

11. Summary of Supposed Benefits

Replacing prisons with non-carceral, rehabilitation- and community-based models is claimed to:

  • Reduce overall harm (trauma, family disruption, community destabilization).
  • Improve long-term safety by addressing root causes and promoting genuine behavior change.
  • Better support survivors, centering their needs and voices.
  • Advance racial and social justice, challenging systems that criminalize poverty and marginalization.
  • Use resources more effectively, redirecting funds from cages to care, housing, and opportunity.
  • Empower communities, shifting safety from a state-imposed system to a collective practice.
  • Align with human rights and dignity, limiting coercion and honoring people’s capacity to change.
  • Encourage creative, context-specific responses to harm instead of one-size-fits-all punishment.

These are the core reasons advocates give for moving away from prisons entirely and building non-carceral systems of justice and safety.

“If We Don’t Cage Everybody, How Will We Be Safe?”

A Helpful Guide for People Deeply In Love With Prisons

In an age of climate collapse, skyrocketing inequality, and billionaires launching vanity rockets into space, many people are asking hard questions about the prison system. This guide is for them: the loyal supporters of mass incarceration who know that no matter how many studies, statistics, or ruined lives pile up, the real problem is not the cages—it’s everyone who wants fewer cages.

Let us analyze their logic with all the seriousness it deserves.

Step 1: Confuse “Prisons” With “Literally The Only Possible Response To Harm”

Abolitionists: “Maybe we should invest in housing, mental health care, education, harm reduction, and restorative justice instead of defaulting to cages.”

Prison Defenders: “So you want chaos. Got it.”

It’s a beautifully simple worldview: humans can only be dealt with in two ways—

  1. Lock them in a box.
  2. Utter, lawless anarchy where people duel in the streets with shopping carts.

There is nothing in between. No mediation, no community accountability, no non-carceral responses, no social services. Just Concrete Box or Mad Max. If anyone suggests options 3 through 10,000, they are clearly “naive” and “don’t understand how the world really works.”

A small technicality: to defend prisons, you have to not examine prisons.

You must master the technique of speaking about “public safety” while delicately ignoring:

  • Sky-high recidivism rates
  • The fact that prisons often function as graduate schools for violence and trauma
  • That people exit prison with fewer resources, more mental health struggles, and fewer legal ways to survive

The key is to treat “We locked them up” as a mic-drop solution, rather than “We temporarily stored a traumatized person in a warehouse with other traumatized people, then released them with less support and more stigma.”

This is called “being tough on crime” instead of “being very bad at cause and effect.”

Step 3: Ignore That Rich People Don’t Experience “Justice” The Same Way

Prisons, we’re told, are about “consequences” and “accountability.”

Curious, then, that if you steal a car, you might spend years in prison. But if you steal wages from hundreds of workers, dump toxic sludge into a river, or help crash the global economy, your harsh punishment is…a fine, a consulting gig, and a podcast.

We are assured this is not hypocrisy. It’s just that:

  • Street crime = moral failing that must be crushed with lifelong punishment.
  • Corporate crime = unfortunate mistake that can be dealt with via sternly worded memo and maybe community service where executives give TED Talks about “learning from failure.”

If you point this out, you’re told that abolitionists “don’t care about victims.” Victims, apparently, only count when harm is done by poor people and not by powerful institutions.

Defenders often insist, “Prisons are about rehabilitation!” This is a touching statement, on par with “The Amazon warehouse is about relaxation and personal growth.”

They imagine prisons as:

  • Cozy campuses
  • Full of therapy, classes, job training
  • All leading to successful re-entry into society

In reality, many prisons:

  • Cut education programs
  • Provide minimal or no counseling
  • Offer “job training” for jobs that don’t exist when you’re out, or won’t hire you because of your record

And then when people struggle after release, we’re told it proves they’re inherently dangerous and irredeemable—as opposed to, say, victims of a system deliberately designed to set them up to fail.

It’s a perfect loop:
Create conditions that make it nearly impossible to rebuild your life → blame the individual for failing → use that “failure” to defend more prisons.

Elegant, in a very dystopian way.

Step 5: Treat “Safety” As Something You Manufacture With Bars, Not With Resources

Abolitionists say: “You know what actually reduces harm? Stable housing, healthcare, addiction treatment, mental health services, good schools, and living-wage jobs.”

Defenders respond: “That sounds expensive. Anyway, here’s a $500 million proposal for a new mega-jail.”

The operating theory:

  • A dollar spent on social services is “unserious” and “utopian.”
  • A dollar spent on cages is “realistic” and “responsible.”

You can’t measure the crimes that never happened because someone had support; you can measure the size of a new prison, and it’s big, which makes people feel something is being done.

Who needs evidence of effectiveness when you have 1,000 more beds and a ribbon-cutting ceremony?

Any time abolition is discussed, someone invokes The Hypothetical Most Evil Person Alive:

“But what about the serial killer who also kicks puppies, burns libraries, and never recycles? Checkmate.”

Never mind that:

  • They represent a tiny fraction of people in cages, and
  • We already don’t handle them particularly well, ethically, or effectively.

Our current system responds to nearly every kind of harm—from addiction-related theft to complex mental illness to domestic violence—with one tool: imprisonment. And then, when that tool predictably fails, we conclude we just need more of it.

It’s like treating every medical condition with leeches and, when people die, declaring: “Clearly we didn’t use enough leeches. Also, I find this ‘abolish leeches’ talk very troubling.”

Abolitionists say, “Let’s design an entirely different set of responses, including for the tiny portion of people who do serious, repeated harm.”
Prison defenders reply, “Why would we consider new tools when the old one is failing so reliably?”

Step 7: Weaponize Victims’ Pain To Protect Institutions, Then Forget Victims Again

The script goes like this:

  1. Someone experienced a terrible harm.
  2. An abolitionist says, “We should center survivors’ needs: safety, healing, restitution, and prevention.”
  3. A defender says, “How dare you speak about victims—you just want criminals to roam free!”

This is the same system that:

  • Rarely gives survivors meaningful say in outcomes
  • Often leaves survivors with no practical support beyond “you can testify at trial”
  • Doesn’t provide long-term counseling, housing, or financial assistance for most victims

But suddenly their pain becomes a rhetorical shield to protect…prisons. Not survivors. Not healing. Just the existing machinery.

If survivors ask for something other than cages—like therapy, relocation, mediation, or community accountability—they’re quietly ignored because that doesn’t fit the script.

Step 8: Pretend “Abolition” Means “Flip A Giant Switch Tomorrow And Unlock Every Door”

To win any debate, you must first completely misrepresent your opponent. Enter the classic:

“So you want to let everyone out tomorrow and hope for the best.”

No gradual defunding of cages while funding alternatives.
No experimentation with community-based interventions.
No transition periods, pilot programs, expanded restorative and transformative justice practices.

Just one big cartoon lever labeled “PRISONS: ON / OFF.”

This makes abolitionists sound like they woke up one morning and said, “What if we replaced all laws with vibes?” It’s much easier to caricature people as reckless idealists than to engage with their actual proposals about stepwise system transformation.

You’ll hear: “People must be held accountable for their choices.”

Reasonable. But the same people often have little interest in:

  • Holding housing policy accountable for mass homelessness
  • Holding the healthcare system accountable for untreated mental illness and addiction
  • Holding schools accountable for funneling kids into police and suspensions instead of support
  • Holding economic policy accountable for desperation and survival crimes

Accountability stops the moment we move from “person who shoplifted” to “multi-billion-dollar structures that made it easier to end up with nothing than with enough.”

The moral:

  • When a poor person harms, it’s an individual failing.
  • When a system harms millions, it’s “complicated” and “not the time to point fingers.”

Defenders often concede: “Of course the system has flaws. Of course there’s bias. Of course racism plays a role. We just need reforms—not abolition.”

They then propose reforms like:

  • Nicer uniforms for guards
  • A mindfulness app
  • Maybe a mural

Meanwhile:

  • Black, Indigenous, and other marginalized communities remain disproportionately targeted, policed, caged, and killed.
  • Prisons continue to warehouse mental illness, disability, and poverty.
  • Private companies profit from everything from prison labor to phone calls that cost more per minute than a luxury cruise.

If a system consistently targets the same people, for generations, at massive scale, with predictable results, maybe it’s not “broken.” Maybe it’s functioning as intended.

Abolition doesn’t say, “Nothing wrong here.” It says, “This is working too well at doing the wrong thing.”

Conclusion: The Real Radical Idea Is Believing This Is The Best We Can Do

Abolitionists are often called “radical” and “unrealistic” for believing humans are capable of something better than endless cages.

Yet it’s somehow not radical to believe:

  • We can afford infinite prisons, but not universal healthcare or housing.
  • We can imagine self-driving cars and colonizing Mars, but not a justice system that doesn’t rely primarily on punishment and exile.
